title: Is Your ERP Ready for PINT AE? Dynamics 365 and the UAE E-Invoicing Mandate
metaTitle: PINT AE requirements, UAE e-invoicing in Dynamics 365 | Rounak Computers | Rounak Computers LLC
excerpt: PINT AE requirements explained for Dynamics 365 users: check your ERP is ready for the UAE e-invoicing mandate with Rounak Computers, a Microsoft Gold partner.

sections.heading: PINT AE requirements, in plain terms
paragraphs: PINT AE (Peppol International Invoice, UAE) is the structured XML format every in-scope invoice and credit note must follow under the UAE's Electronic Invoicing System. A PDF emailed to a customer, or a scanned paper invoice, no longer counts once your phase goes live. Your ERP has to produce complete, correct invoice data. An Accredited Service Provider (ASP) then validates that data, converts it to PINT AE where needed, delivers it over the Peppol network and reports the tax data to the Federal Tax Authority (FTA).

For companies running Microsoft Dynamics 365, the practical question is whether your current version, master data, tax setup and integrations can feed that chain without manual fixes. The Ministry of Finance's specification lists 51 mandatory fields for a PINT AE tax invoice. Most readiness problems start in the ERP, long before an invoice reaches the ASP.
Scope

sections.heading: Who the UAE e-invoicing mandate covers
points: B2B and B2G transactions, invoices and credit notes exchanged between businesses and with government entities, subject to specific exclusions set out in the framework.
VAT registration is not the trigger, the mandate applies to persons conducting business in the UAE, so non-registered businesses that issue in-scope invoices should check their position.
Large businesses first, companies with annual revenue of AED 50 million or more form the first mandatory wave.
All other businesses next, companies below AED 50 million follow in the second wave, then in-scope government entities.
Pilot participants, a selected group began on 1 July 2026, and participants are temporarily exempt from penalties during the pilot.
Both sides of the invoice, suppliers must be able to issue PINT AE invoices, and buyers must be able to receive and store them through their own ASP.

sections.heading: The dates that matter
paragraphs: The legal basis is Ministerial Decisions No. 243 and No. 244 of 2025. In May 2026 the Ministry of Finance amended Decision 244 and moved the ASP appointment deadline for large businesses from 31 July to 30 October 2026. The go-live date did not move. The timeline below reflects the position as of 6 October 2026.
points: 1 July 2026 Pilot phase begins Selected taxpayers test the system ahead of mandatory enforcement.
30 October 2026 Large businesses appoint an ASP Applies to revenue of AED 50 million or more. This was moved from the original 31 July 2026 date.
1 January 2027 Large businesses go live PINT AE invoices must be sent and received through the Electronic Invoicing System.
31 March 2027 Everyone else appoints an ASP Applies to businesses below AED 50 million and to in-scope government entities.
1 July 2027 Remaining businesses go live The second business wave becomes subject to mandatory e-invoicing.
1 October 2027 Government entities go live B2G e-invoicing becomes mandatory for in-scope government bodies.

sections.heading: How an e-invoice travels from Dynamics 365 to your customer
paragraphs: The UAE uses a Peppol-based, decentralised "five-corner" model. Dynamics 365 sits at corner one. Your ERP never talks to the FTA directly. Every invoice passes through accredited providers who carry legal responsibility for validation and exchange.

sections.heading: Dynamics 365 creates the invoice
paragraphs: Posting a sales, free text or project invoice produces the structured data: parties, TRNs, lines, VAT and totals.

sections.heading: Your ASP validates it
paragraphs: The ASP checks the data against PINT AE rules, converts it to PINT AE XML if needed and rejects anything incomplete.

sections.heading: The buyer's ASP delivers it
paragraphs: The invoice crosses the Peppol network to the buyer's ASP, which passes it into the buyer's own system.

sections.heading: Tax data reaches the FTA
paragraphs: Required tax data is reported to the FTA platform (corner five), and status messages flow back to your ERP.
Invoice data

sections.heading: What PINT AE needs from your invoice data
paragraphs: PINT AE is built on the international Peppol PINT model (UBL 2.1 under the hood) with a UAE-specific layer for local VAT rules. The data dictionary holds more than 135 elements across mandatory, conditional and optional fields. The 51 mandatory fields for a tax invoice fall into a few groups your ERP must fill every time.
points: Invoice details: number, issue date, invoice type and currency
Seller and buyer identity, including Tax Registration Numbers (TRNs)
Line items with quantities, prices and recognised unit-of-measure codes
VAT breakdown by tax category, plus document totals and amount due
Credit notes in the same structured format, linked to the original invoice
Electronic archiving of records for at least five years

sections.heading: How Dynamics 365 supports PINT AE compliance
paragraphs: Microsoft Dynamics 365 already holds most of what a PINT AE invoice needs: customers, items, tax codes and posted transactions. Compliance comes from shaping that data correctly and connecting it to an ASP. Dynamics 365 is not itself an ASP. Here is where each part of the work happens.

sections.heading: VAT and invoice data
paragraphs: Sales tax groups, item tax groups and customer TRNs determine the VAT category and amounts that land in each PINT AE field.

sections.heading: Structured e-invoicing
paragraphs: In Finance and Supply Chain Management, Electronic Reporting (ER) configurations and the Electronic invoicing service turn posted invoices into structured XML.

sections.heading: Validation
paragraphs: Mandatory fields, tax categories and number sequences can be checked before posting, so the ASP rejects fewer documents.

sections.heading: Status and reporting
paragraphs: Two-way communication returns accepted or rejected statuses to the ERP, giving finance one place to track every document.

sections.heading: ASP integration
paragraphs: An ASP connector or API carries invoices out of Dynamics 365 and onto the Peppol network as the last-mile link.

sections.heading: Archiving
paragraphs: Submitted XML and responses need to be retained and retrievable for audit, either in the ERP, the ASP platform or both.

sections.heading: Dynamics 365 Finance, Business Central and legacy versions compared
paragraphs: "Dynamics 365" covers very different products, and the route to PINT AE depends on which one you run. Microsoft has announced built-in UAE e-invoicing for Dynamics 365 Finance. It covers B2B and B2G invoices and credit notes from sales orders, free text invoices and project invoices, sent in PINT XML over Peppol with an ASP as the last-mile connector. Its release timing has shifted between update waves, so confirm the current status on Microsoft's roadmap for your exact version before you plan around it.

If you are still on AX 2012 or NAV, the mandate is a good moment to weigh a short-term connector against moving the ERP to the cloud. A connector bought only to meet the 2027 deadline may cost more over three years than the upgrade it postpones.

sections.heading: PINT AE readiness checklist for Dynamics 365
paragraphs: Run through this with finance and IT in the same room. Any item you cannot answer with confidence becomes a work item before your ASP deadline.
points: ERP version: on a supported, current Dynamics 365 release
ERP version: cloud or on-premises status confirmed
Master data: valid TRNs on every UAE customer and vendor
Master data: addresses, emirates and legal names cleaned
Tax configuration: every VAT scenario mapped to a PINT AE tax category
Tax configuration: zero-rated, exempt and reverse-charge cases tested
Invoice formats: sales, free text, project invoices and credit notes covered
Invoice formats: units of measure mapped to recognised codes
Integrations: ASP shortlisted, appointed and connected
Integrations: third-party billing systems feeding the same flow
Workflows: owners for rejected invoices and status monitoring
Workflows: archiving and audit retrieval agreed

sections.heading: Common implementation mistakes, and what good looks like
points: Treating e-invoicing as a finance project and bringing IT in late.
Choosing an ASP on price before checking how it connects to your Dynamics version.
Mapping only the standard tax invoice and forgetting credit notes and project billing.
Assuming the ASP will fix bad customer TRNs and missing fields.
Counting the ASP appointment as the finish line instead of the start of testing.
A joint finance, tax and IT owner group from the first workshop.
ASP selection driven by integration fit, support model and Peppol certification.
Every invoice type and VAT scenario tested end to end before go-live.
Master data cleaned in the ERP, where the error starts.
Testing time reserved between ASP appointment and the go-live date.

sections.heading: After go-live: system failures and the two-business-day rule
paragraphs: Most guides end at go-live, but the mandate keeps applying afterwards. Under Cabinet Decision No. 106 of 2025, a "system failure" includes ASP outages, network disruptions and software faults. Any failure that stops you issuing or receiving e-invoices must be reported to the FTA within two business days.
Late notification of a system failure carries a penalty of AED 1,000 for each day of delay.

In practice, someone has to watch the connector, the ASP status feed and the ERP job queue, and must know who files the notice. That is an IT operations duty as much as a tax one. Monitoring, alerting and escalation should be part of your managed support arrangement. Because invoice data now leaves the ERP for external platforms, it is also worth checking where your ASP stores and processes that data against UAE data localization and privacy rules.
Penalties

sections.heading: What non-compliance costs
paragraphs: Preparation
points: Failure to implement on time, including not appointing an ASP by the deadline: AED 5,000 for each month of delay or part of a month.
Late e-invoices: AED 100 per invoice, capped at AED 5,000 per month.
Late electronic credit notes: AED 100 per credit note, capped at AED 5,000 per month.
Late notice of a system failure: AED 1,000 for each day of delay.

sections.heading: Assess your current state
paragraphs: Confirm your Dynamics version and revenue cohort, then measure current invoices against the 51 mandatory fields.

sections.heading: Fix data and tax setup
paragraphs: Clean TRNs and addresses, then map every VAT scenario and unit of measure to its PINT AE value.

sections.heading: Choose and appoint an ASP
paragraphs: Shortlist accredited, Peppol-certified providers that fit your Dynamics edition, and appoint before your deadline.

sections.heading: Build, test, then go live
paragraphs: Connect the ERP, test every invoice type with real scenarios, train staff on rejections and set up monitoring.

sections.heading: Better ASP choice
paragraphs: ASP capacity is finite. Early movers compare integration fit and pricing instead of signing whatever is still available in December.

sections.heading: Real testing time
paragraphs: The deadline extension gave more time to appoint an ASP, not to build. Starting now protects the weeks needed for end-to-end testing.

sections.heading: Cleaner finance data
paragraphs: Master data and tax fixes made for PINT AE also improve VAT returns, reconciliations and reporting long after go-live.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions
paragraphs: Every in-scope invoice and credit note must be issued as structured XML that follows the PINT AE data model, including the 51 mandatory fields for a tax invoice. It must be sent through an Accredited Service Provider over the Peppol network, with tax data reported to the FTA. PDFs and paper invoices are not compliant once your phase goes live.

VAT registration is not the trigger. The mandate applies to persons conducting business in the UAE for in-scope B2B and B2G transactions, subject to specific exclusions. A non-registered business issuing such invoices should confirm its position with a tax adviser.

No. Dynamics 365 produces the invoice data, but transmission must go through an Accredited Service Provider. The ASP validates the invoice, delivers it to the buyer's ASP over Peppol and reports the tax data to the FTA. Dynamics 365 is not an ASP.

Business Central includes an E-Documents framework for electronic document exchange. For UAE PINT AE, businesses currently rely on an extension or an ASP connector that maps invoice data to the mandatory fields. Check the current localisation status for your version before choosing a route.

Yes, but not through Microsoft's Electronic invoicing service, which does not support on-premises deployments. You would need middleware or an ASP integration built around your existing system, or an upgrade to a cloud version of Dynamics 365. Compare the cost of both over several years rather than only against the deadline.

An outage that prevents you from issuing or receiving e-invoices counts as a system failure. It must be reported to the FTA within two business days, and late notification carries a penalty of AED 1,000 per day of delay. Monitoring and a clear escalation owner should be in place before go-live.

Businesses with annual revenue of AED 50 million or more must appoint an ASP by 30 October 2026 and go live on 1 January 2027. Businesses below that threshold and in-scope government entities must appoint an ASP by 31 March 2027. Those businesses go live on 1 July 2027, and government entities on 1 October 2027.

sections.heading: Not sure where your Dynamics 365 stands?
paragraphs: Rounak Computers has supported UAE businesses from Bur Dubai since 2004 as a Microsoft Gold partner with certified in-house engineers. We can review your ERP version, master data, tax configuration and integrations against PINT AE, then support the implementation and the monitoring after go-live.

title: Understanding Data Localization and Privacy Laws in the UAE in 2026
metaTitle: UAE Data Localization & Privacy Law 2026 Guide | Rounak Computers | Rounak Computers LLC
excerpt: Understand UAE data localization rules, PDPL & cross-border transfer obligations for 2026. Learn infrastructure & compliance steps your IT team can act on today.
intro: In 2026, the question of "where the data lives and who manages it" is turning from a technical detail into a strategic decision. The UAE has a multi-level regulatory system: the federal PDPL law, separate regimes in financial zones, and sectoral regulations for banking and medical data. To ignore this is to accept legal and operational risks that directly affect the cost of IT ownership and reputation. Below is a summary of what is important to consider and how Rounak Computers helps build a test-resistant architecture.

sections.heading: Regulatory Map: Federation, Free zones, and Industry rules
paragraphs: Federal Decree-Law No. 45/2021 (PDPL) entered into force on January 2, 2022, with enforcement related to the executive regulations and the role of the UAE Data Office as a regulator and a source of clarification. The law also applies to controllers/processors outside the country if they process personal data of UAE residents.

DIFC and ADGM have their own detailed GDPR-like regimes with real-world cases and penalties: in DIFC, administrative fines under Schedule 2 (10-100 thousand USD), in ADGM, the administrative fine ceiling can reach 28 million USD.

Industry requirements tighten localization: The Central Bank is obliged to store customer and payment data in the country, and in the medical sector, electronic medical data cannot be moved outside the UAE except in specially authorized cases. The shelf life for payment services is at least 5 years, and notification of a breakdown in card schemes must be within 72 hours.

sections.heading: What is Considered Localization and Cross-Border Transfer?
paragraphs: At the level of the mainland jurisdiction, data export is permissible with adequate protection of the host country; a similar logic applies in the DIFC/ADGM: lists of adequate jurisdictions are published by their authorized bodies. Exceptions at the federal level relate primarily to healthcare.

In practice, this means three control loops: where the data is stored, how and on what legal grounds it is transferred, and what technical measures are applied throughout the lifecycle. In this context, cloud solutions in UAE and cloud service providers in Dubai play an important role, allowing companies to host data in the country, respecting localization standards and providing flexibility for scaling.

sections.heading: Rights of Subjects and Obligations of Companies
paragraphs: The PDPL introduces rights to access, correct, and delete data, obligations to record processing operations, DPIA for high-risk scenarios, DPO assignment, consent management, and breakdown notification.

The terms and procedures for notification are detailed in the DIFC/ADGM: in the ADGM, a message to the regulator within 72 hours, and if necessary, informing the subjects. Penalties are provided for failure to notify.

sections.heading: Responsibility and Sanctions
paragraphs: Under the PDPL, administrative fines are set by the Data Office (the amounts are specified in the regulations); in parallel, criminal law standards apply: for unlawful disclosure of data, a fine of at least 20,000 AED and up to a year in prison. Under the Cybercrime Law, fines can reach 5,000,000 AED depending on the nature of the offense.

sections.heading: Security and Operational Sustainability
paragraphs: The key task is to ensure information security in Dubai at the process and infrastructure level: access control, data encryption "at rest" and "in transit", audit of actions and regular recovery tests. These measures minimize the risks of leakage and ensure full compliance with PDPL requirements. Companies can additionally conclude an IT annual maintenance contract in Dubai to standardize SLAs and fix the responsibility for maintenance.

For an integrated approach, it is worth involving it maintenance companies in dubai, which will provide technical audits, updates and support in compliance with legal requirements and security standards.

sections.heading: Compliance Plan for an IT Leader: 8 Mandatory Steps
points: Classify the data and flow maps. Identify personal and sensitive kits, and describe cross-border routes and reasons for transfer.
Implement the principles of privacy by design. Minimize collection and retention periods, and implement access control mechanisms.
Encryption and control. Use end-to-end encryption, RBAC/ABAC role models, and regular recovery checks.
Consent management. Set up transparent mechanics for obtaining and revoking consent.
DPIA and DPO. Conduct risk assessments and appoint responsible specialists.
Incident preparedness. Enable notification schedules (72 hours) and internal response procedures.
Sectoral exceptions. Banking and medical data are subject to mandatory localization.
Contracts and outsourcing. Specify processing, security, and notification requirements in the contracts.

sections.heading: How Rounak Computers Adds Value
paragraphs: Rounak Computers helps companies implement compliance principles not on paper, but in real infrastructure. We are building a PDPL/DIFC/ADGM compliance architecture: data classification and inventory, stream configuration, encryption and backup. Using cloud service providers in Dubai, on-premises clouds, and services like Microsoft Azure UAE, we provide data control, fault tolerance, and process transparency.

Compliance in the UAE is not a formality, but a strategic element of IT management. Localization and privacy are becoming a characteristic of architecture: where data is stored, how it is transmitted, and how it is protected. Start with a data map, assess the risks, and build an infrastructure that combines technology, security, and the law. Rounak Computers is ready to accompany this path so that the business meets the requirements and continues to develop at no extra cost.

title: Why Your New Office Wi-Fi Fails at 4pm: AP Placement, Density and Backhaul
metaTitle: Office wifi performance issues and AP placement | Rounak Computers | Rounak Computers LLC
excerpt: Office wifi performance issues late in the day often come from poor AP placement, user density or weak backhaul. Rounak Computers engineers explain the fixes.

sections.heading: The 4pm slowdown is a capacity problem, not a signal problem
paragraphs: If your Wi-Fi feels fine at 9am and falls apart late in the afternoon, coverage is rarely the culprit. Laptops still show full bars. What has changed is how many devices are talking at once, how much airtime each access point (AP) has left to share, and how much traffic the wired network behind those APs can carry.

Most office Wi-Fi performance issues in a new fit-out trace back to three design decisions. This guide explains each one in plain terms, shows how to tell which one is hurting you, and covers when it makes sense to bring in a professional site survey.
Why late afternoon
points: Placement: APs mounted for even coverage on the ceiling plan, not for where people actually sit, meet and call.
Density: more phones, laptops and video calls per AP than the original design assumed.
Backhaul: switch ports, PoE budgets and uplinks that cap what the Wi-Fi can deliver.

sections.heading: What happens to your office network between 9am and 4pm
paragraphs: Peak-hour Wi-Fi problems build up through the day. Load stacks on load until the weakest link gives way, and in many offices that tipping point lands in the final stretch before people head home.
Coverage tells you whether a device can connect. Capacity tells you whether everyone can work at the same time. A new office can pass the first test and fail the second.
Root causes
points: 9:00 Staff arrive and devices join Laptops, phones, tablets and watches associate within minutes of each other. Most people bring more than one Wi-Fi device, so the real client count is well above headcount.
11:00 Meeting rooms fill up Teams and Zoom calls need steady, low-latency airtime in both directions. A full room pulls that from the nearest AP, which is often also serving the desks outside.

14:00 Background traffic piles on OneDrive and SharePoint sync, operating system updates, cloud backups and large attachments run alongside live work. Nobody sees this traffic, yet it competes for the same channels.

16:00 Everything overlaps End-of-day calls, uploads and deadline pushes coincide with neighbouring offices hitting their own peak on nearby channels. Airtime, PoE headroom and uplinks reach their limits together.

sections.heading: The six causes behind most office Wi-Fi performance issues
paragraphs: Wi-Fi is a shared medium. On any one channel, devices take turns to transmit, so anything that adds devices, slows them down or adds noise makes everyone wait longer. These are the six patterns that come up again and again in busy offices.

sections.heading: AP overload
paragraphs: Each AP radio splits its airtime across every client attached to it. When a desk cluster and a meeting room both lean on the same AP, every device spends more time waiting and less time sending.

sections.heading: Channel congestion
paragraphs: APs on the same channel that can hear each other share airtime as if they were one AP. Running every AP at full power, or using wide 80 or 160 MHz channels on a tight floor, makes this worse rather than better.

sections.heading: Interference
paragraphs: Neighbouring company networks, phone hotspots, wireless presentation dongles, Bluetooth and the pantry microwave all add noise. In shared towers and business centres, the neighbours tend to peak at the same hour you do.

sections.heading: Poor AP placement
paragraphs: APs hidden above metal ceiling tiles, lined up along corridors or tucked into the comms room reach users through glass partitions, concrete lift cores and filing walls. Signal arrives, but at slow data rates.

sections.heading: Backhaul bottlenecks
paragraphs: The Wi-Fi can only move what the cabling, switch ports, PoE budget, firewall and internet circuit behind it allow. A fast AP on a slow or underpowered port behaves like a slow AP.

sections.heading: Slow and legacy clients
paragraphs: Older 2.4 GHz devices and laptops sitting far from their AP connect at low data rates. They need more airtime to send the same data, which slows every other device on that radio.
Placement

sections.heading: AP placement: design for where people sit, meet and call
paragraphs: In many new offices, APs are positioned from the ceiling plan to give an even grid of coverage across the floor. That works on handover day when the space is empty. Once teams move in, the load is anything but even: a sales bay, a boardroom and a breakout area can each generate more traffic than the rest of the floor combined.
points: APs spaced evenly, regardless of seating density.
Meeting rooms served by an AP outside the glass wall.
Every AP at maximum power, overlapping its neighbours.
AP count based on floor area alone.
More APs where people cluster, fewer in storage and corridors.
Busy meeting and training rooms get their own AP.
Lower transmit power, so each AP serves a smaller, busier cell.
AP count based on peak concurrent devices and the apps they run.

sections.heading: How this plays out in three common office spaces
Open-plan floors
paragraphs: Long benches of hot desks put dozens of laptops within range of one or two APs. Add phones on the same SSID and the airtime runs out long before the signal does. Splitting the floor into smaller cells with more APs at lower power usually helps more than buying a faster AP.

sections.heading: Meeting rooms
paragraphs: A boardroom of people on a hybrid call can swamp a shared AP within minutes. Glass walls and coated façade glazing also weaken signal from outside the room. A dedicated ceiling AP inside larger rooms keeps calls stable and stops one meeting slowing the desks next door.

sections.heading: Coworking and business centres
paragraphs: Many companies share one building, often one network, and every tenant brings their own devices and hotspots. Here, channel planning, client isolation and per-tenant VLANs matter as much as AP count, and congestion from neighbours is part of the design brief.
Bands and channels

sections.heading: Getting 5 GHz and 6 GHz to carry the load
paragraphs: The frequency band a device uses has a big effect on how crowded its airspace is. The 2.4 GHz band has very few non-overlapping channels and travels far, so it collects interference from every neighbour. 5 GHz offers many more channels, and 6 GHz, available to Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 devices, adds clean spectrum that older clients cannot use at all.

In a dense office, narrower channels often beat wider ones. Using 20 or 40 MHz channels on 5 GHz gives you more separate channels to spread across APs, which cuts co-channel contention. Wide 80 or 160 MHz channels look impressive on a single-laptop speed test, but they leave neighbouring APs fighting over the same slice of spectrum when the floor is full.

UAE note: the regulator designated 500 MHz of the 6 GHz band, 5925-6425 MHz, for indoor Wi-Fi at 250 mW EIRP under class authorization in December 2020. That lower-power, indoor-only allocation means 6 GHz cells are smaller than many installers expect, so 6 GHz designs need APs closer to users. The 500 MHz block also fits only one contiguous 320 MHz channel, so Wi-Fi 7 in a UAE office should be planned around narrower channels.
Backhaul
points: Steer capable clients up: use band steering so modern laptops and phones land on 5 or 6 GHz.
Keep 2.4 GHz small: reserve it for printers, sensors and older devices that need it.
Check auto channel settings: radio resource management helps, but verify its choices against a real scan at peak time.
Plan for WPA3 on 6 GHz: 6 GHz networks require WPA3, so older security settings and some legacy devices need a separate SSID.

sections.heading: The wired network behind your Wi-Fi
paragraphs: Backhaul is everything between the AP and the internet: the cable run, the switch port, the power that port supplies, the uplink from that switch, the firewall and the internet circuit. It is the part most Wi-Fi complaints ignore, and it is the part that fails quietly, because a starved AP still broadcasts a strong signal.

If your office is still in fit-out, the cheapest moment to fix backhaul is before the ceilings close. Planning structured cabling for the office with a dedicated run to every AP location, including spare points in meeting rooms, avoids reopening ceiling tiles later just to add one AP.
Diagnosis
points: Component
What limits it
How it shows up at peak
AP uplink port
Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 APs can push more than a 1 Gbps port carries. Multi-gig ports (2.5 or 5 GbE) and suitable cabling remove that ceiling.
Busy APs flatline at the same throughput no matter how many clients you move.
PoE budget
Each switch has a total power budget, and each port a PoE class (802.3af, at or bt). Many enterprise APs run in a reduced mode when underpowered, switching off a radio or spatial streams.
Some APs perform worse than identical models elsewhere on the floor, often the last ones added.
Switch uplinks
Many APs and wired desks share one uplink to the core switch or firewall. Heavy oversubscription turns it into a queue.
Wired and wireless users slow down together on the same floor or switch stack.
Firewall
Throughput drops when inspection, IPS and SSL decryption are switched on, and rated figures are usually measured without them.
The whole office slows at once, with firewall CPU running high during the busiest hour.
Internet circuit
Bandwidth that was right for the old headcount, or a single link carrying guests, cloud backups and calls together.
Speed tests from a cabled PC are slow too, and uploads suffer before downloads.

sections.heading: Symptom checker: which bottleneck is it?
paragraphs: Different causes leave different fingerprints. Match what your staff report to the most likely cause, then run the quick check before spending money on new hardware.
Troubleshooting

Walk test along the route, noting signal and AP changes at each handoff.
One meeting room is always bad
No AP in the room, glass or solid walls in the way

sections.heading: Troubleshooting office Wi-Fi in four steps
paragraphs: You do not need specialist tools to narrow the problem down. These steps take a few days of observation and separate wireless issues from wired ones.

sections.heading: Log when and where
paragraphs: Ask staff to note the time, location and app each time Wi-Fi feels slow. Patterns by hour and by zone point straight at the cause.

sections.heading: Read the controller at peak
paragraphs: Compare client counts, channel utilisation and retry rates per AP at 4pm against the morning. Overloaded APs stand out quickly.

sections.heading: Split wireless from wired
paragraphs: Plug a laptop into the same switch as a struggling AP and test at peak. If the cabled test is also slow, the problem sits behind the Wi-Fi.

sections.heading: Check the edge
paragraphs: Review firewall load, uplink graphs and internet utilisation for the same hour. Background jobs scheduled for the afternoon often show up here.

If nobody in the office has access to the Wi-Fi controller, or the readings do not line up with what users report, an experienced IT support team in Dubai can pull the logs, compare peak and off-peak data and tell you whether you are looking at an AP, RF or backhaul problem before anything is replaced.
High-density offices

sections.heading: Recommendations for busy floors
paragraphs: These practices apply whether you are planning a fresh fit-out or fixing a network that already struggles. They work best together, since an extra AP on a congested channel or an underpowered port will not deliver what you paid for.
If no one in-house owns the network day to day, managed IT services can cover monitoring, firmware and capacity reviews as headcount changes.
Site surveys
points: Size AP count from peak concurrent devices and apps, not floor area alone
Give large meeting and training rooms their own ceiling AP
Mount APs close to users, clear of metal tiles, ducts and lift cores
Lower transmit power so cells are smaller and busier
Use 20 or 40 MHz channels on 5 GHz in dense zones
Enable 6 GHz for Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 laptops
Keep 2.4 GHz for the devices that truly need it
Separate staff, guest and IoT traffic onto their own VLANs
Limit the number of SSIDs per radio to cut beacon overhead
Apply QoS so voice and video get priority
Run multi-gig uplinks and confirm PoE budget per switch
Leave headroom for visitors and future hiring

sections.heading: When a professional Wi-Fi site survey is worth it
paragraphs: Troubleshooting tells you what is wrong today. A site survey tells you what the space can support and where every AP should go. A predictive survey models the floor plan and wall materials before installation. An on-site survey measures real signal, interference and throughput with the office in use, and a validation survey after installation confirms the design works at peak.

Wi-Fi capacity also drifts over time as staff, devices and cloud apps change. Covering the network under an IT AMC in Dubai keeps firmware current and puts someone on watch for the slow creep that turns into a 4pm complaint.
FAQ
points: Before a move or fit-out: surveying from drawings costs far less than recabling after handover.
After headcount grows: a design sized for the original team rarely survives a much larger one.
When fixes have not stuck: if extra APs or a faster internet plan made no lasting difference, the problem needs measuring, not guessing.
In shared or difficult buildings: coworking floors, glass-heavy towers and concrete cores need RF measured on site.
For critical spaces: clinics, classrooms and boardrooms where dropped calls or devices carry a real cost.

sections.heading: Office Wi-Fi performance questions
paragraphs: Load builds through the day. By late afternoon, the most devices are connected, meeting rooms are busiest, background sync and updates are running, and neighbouring offices are at their own peak. The network was usually designed for coverage rather than this combined load, so APs, channels or uplinks run out of capacity together.

Only if the internet circuit is the bottleneck. Test from a cabled PC at peak time: if wired speeds are fine but Wi-Fi is slow, the problem is AP capacity, RF congestion or placement, and a bigger plan will not help. If wired speeds are also slow, look at the circuit, firewall and switch uplinks.

The maximum client figure on a datasheet is a connection limit, not a comfortable working load. Real capacity depends on the AP model, its radios, the bands clients use, how far away they sit and what they are doing. A few people on video calls consume far more airtime than many people reading email, so size APs for peak concurrent activity rather than headcount.

Mesh units send their backhaul over the air, which uses the same airtime your users need. That can work in small spaces where cabling is impossible, but in a busy office, APs with wired backhaul to a PoE switch perform far more consistently under load.

For dense offices with modern laptops, 6 GHz adds cleaner spectrum and less contention. In the UAE, Wi-Fi can use the lower 500 MHz of the 6 GHz band indoors at 250 mW EIRP, so cells are smaller and AP spacing needs to be tighter. Budget for multi-gig switch ports and enough PoE, otherwise newer APs will be held back by the wired side.

Consider one before a move or fit-out, after significant headcount growth, when earlier fixes have not lasted, or in difficult spaces such as coworking floors, glass-walled towers and buildings with concrete cores. If you cannot say with confidence why the Wi-Fi slows down, a survey replaces guesswork with measurements.

Yes. Any network on the same or overlapping channels within range competes for airtime with yours, even though you cannot see its traffic. In towers and business centres this is common, which is why channel planning, lower transmit power and moving clients to 5 and 6 GHz make such a difference.

title: What Happens to Your Data When You Leave an IT Provider: An Exit Checklist
metaTitle: IT provider exit checklist for safe data handover | Rounak Computers | Rounak Computers LLC
excerpt: IT provider exit checklist: secure data ownership, admin credentials, backups and licences before you switch, with advice from Rounak Computers in Dubai since 2004.

sections.heading: Your data does not leave with the provider, but control can
paragraphs: When you end a contract with an IT provider, nothing automatically happens to your data. Mailboxes stay in your Microsoft 365 tenant, files stay in SharePoint or on your file server, and cloud workloads keep running in Azure, AWS or Huawei Cloud. What changes is who holds the keys. If the provider registered accounts in its own name, kept the only Global Administrator login, or stored your backups in its own vault, you can lose practical access to data you legally own.

A clean exit comes down to three jobs: take full control of every account, take a verified copy of everything the provider holds on your behalf, and get written proof that whatever remains on their side has been securely deleted. This guide covers each job for businesses in Dubai and across the UAE, and finishes with a full IT provider exit checklist you can work through before, during and after the switch.

Ask one question before you give notice: if your provider disappeared tomorrow, could you still log in as an administrator and restore last night's backup? If the answer is no, that is where your exit plan starts.
Data ownership and storage

sections.heading: Where your data actually lives under a managed IT contract
paragraphs: Owning data and controlling it are two different things. Your company owns its emails, customer records and financial files, but a provider that set up your systems may have done so under its own accounts: a cloud subscription billed to the provider, a domain registered with the provider's email address, a backup platform that only the provider can open. None of that changes who owns the information. It does change how easily you can get it back.

Start the exit by mapping each type of data to the place it sits and the person who can actually reach it. The table below shows the pattern we see most often in UAE SMEs and corporates, along with what to request for each.

sections.heading: Data map: what to ask for, by data type
paragraphs: Contract review

sections.heading: Read the contract before you give notice
paragraphs: Your negotiating position is strongest before the provider knows you are leaving. Check these clauses first, so your handover requests match what was actually agreed.

If you are lining up a replacement now, write these exit terms into the new agreement from day one. Our guide to what UAE businesses should demand in an IT support SLA covers the clauses worth negotiating before you sign.
Handover inventory
points: Data ownership. The contract should state that all data, configurations and documentation created for you belong to your business.
Data return. Look for the format, the timeline and whether there is a charge for exporting data or backup copies.
Exit assistance. Check whether handover hours are included, billed separately or missing altogether.
Notice period and renewal. Auto-renewal dates and notice windows decide your real timeline.
Deletion obligations. The provider should commit to deleting your data, including backups, and confirming it in writing.
Licence commitments. Annual licence terms bought through the provider may not be cancellable mid-term, so plan transfers around renewal dates.
Subcontractors and data location. Find out which third parties and which countries were involved in storing your data.

sections.heading: What your outgoing provider should hand back
Access credentials and admin accounts
paragraphs: Global Administrator for Microsoft 365, owner access for Azure, AWS and Huawei Cloud, plus admin logins for firewalls, switches, servers, the domain registrar and every business application.

sections.heading: Backups and encryption keys
paragraphs: A full, current copy of every backup set, the keys needed to decrypt it and the retention history. Ask for it in a format your next data backup service can actually restore.

sections.heading: Data exports
paragraphs: Exports of anything held in the provider's own systems: hosted databases, file shares on their servers, archived mailboxes and old project data.

sections.heading: Third-party integrations
paragraphs: API keys, connectors and service accounts behind your ERP sync, payment gateway, scan-to-email printers, SMTP relays and single sign-on apps. These break quietly when an account is disabled.

sections.heading: IT documentation
paragraphs: Network diagrams, IP plans, firewall rules, runbooks, the password vault export and the full ticket history, including known issues still open at handover.

sections.heading: Licences and asset records
paragraphs: Every software licence with quantities, terms and renewal dates, plus the asset register: laptops, servers, network gear, serial numbers and warranty status.
Data export and migration

sections.heading: Moving data without losing its structure
paragraphs: The best migration is often no migration. If your Microsoft 365 tenant or cloud account is already registered to your company, you usually only need to change who administers it, not move the data anywhere. Migration becomes necessary when the provider hosted data on its own servers or set up accounts in its own name.
When data does have to move, raw files are the easy part. What gets lost is the structure around them:
A planned cloud migration moves a pilot group first, keeps the source untouched until the copy is verified, and has a rollback point if something does not match.
Verification
points: Folder and file permissions, sharing links and group membership
Metadata such as created dates, authors and version history
Mailbox rules, delegated access and shared mailbox settings
Teams chats, channel files and archived records

sections.heading: How to verify data integrity before you sign off
Count and compare
paragraphs: Compare item counts and sizes between source and destination: mailbox items, files per folder, database row counts. For large file transfers, compare checksums so a corrupted file cannot slip through.

sections.heading: Restore something real
paragraphs: A backup report is not proof. Restore a mailbox, a virtual machine and a database copy into a test environment and confirm they open and work. Record what you restored and when.

sections.heading: Let the data owners check
paragraphs: Ask department heads to open the files they rely on. Finance checks closing balances, HR checks employee records, clinics check patient files. They spot gaps an engineer would miss.
Revoking access

sections.heading: Revoke access in the right order
paragraphs: Cutting off the old provider on day one feels safe, but it often locks your own team out of systems nobody else has the passwords for. Cutting them off too late leaves a live door into your network. The order matters more than the speed.
Treat the old provider's access like that of a departing employee with administrator rights: every account, every remote tool and every shared password gets reviewed, not just the ones you remember.

sections.heading: The access revocation sequence
paragraphs: Secure deletion
points: Secure your own way in first. Create business-owned administrator accounts protected by MFA, and confirm the incoming team can log in to every system.
Remove delegated access. Delete the old provider's partner relationship and delegated admin rights in Microsoft 365, plus any cross-account roles in AWS or similar access in Azure and Huawei Cloud.
Disable named accounts. Switch off every account the provider's staff used, including generic ones such as "support" or "itadmin".
Rotate shared secrets. Change service account passwords, API keys, Wi-Fi keys, firewall and VPN credentials, and backup encryption passwords where the platform allows it.
Remove remote tools. Uninstall the old provider's remote monitoring agents, remote desktop tools and VPN profiles from every device.
Check the logs. Review sign-in and audit logs for the following weeks to confirm nothing from the old provider is still connecting.

sections.heading: Secure deletion and written confirmation
paragraphs: Once you hold a verified copy, the provider should delete everything it still keeps: production copies, backup sets, replicas, archives, test environments and exports sitting on staff laptops. Old hard drives they hold for you should be returned or physically destroyed.
Timing matters. Ask for deletion only after your own verification is complete, and only after any records you are legally required to keep are safely held by you or your new provider.

sections.heading: What a deletion confirmation should state
paragraphs: UAE compliance
points: Which data sets were deleted
Every system and backup location covered
Backup copies and replicas included
The deletion or wiping method used
The date deletion was completed
Who carried out the deletion
Any data retained, with the reason
A planned deletion date for retained data
Physical disks returned or destroyed
Signature of an authorised person

sections.heading: UAE privacy and compliance points that shape an exit
Federal PDPL
paragraphs: Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on personal data protection has applied since 2 January 2022 and is supervised by the UAE Data Office. When processing ends, a processor is expected to either erase the personal data or return it to the business that owns it, and liability for a processor's failings can reach back to that business.

sections.heading: DIFC and ADGM
paragraphs: The two financial free zones sit outside the federal law and run their own regimes: the DIFC Data Protection Law No. 5 of 2020 and the ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021. If your company is licensed there, check those rules for data return, deletion and transfers.

sections.heading: Health data
paragraphs: Federal Law No. 2 of 2019 on ICT in health fields generally requires health data to be stored in the UAE and kept for at least 25 years. A clinic changing provider must not let a migration move patient records offshore, or let a deletion request wipe records it is required to keep.

Two practical points follow for every UAE business. First, find out where the old provider kept your backups. Offsite copies are sometimes stored in another country, and you need to know that before you can confirm they were deleted. Second, if your migration routes data through, or to, a location outside the UAE, check the cross-border transfer conditions before the move rather than after. Our overview of data localisation and privacy laws in the UAE explains how these rules fit together.

Government entities and education providers often carry additional security requirements from their own regulators or parent authorities. This guide is practical, not legal advice: for contract disputes or regulated data, involve your legal adviser early.
Exit risks

sections.heading: Common exit risks and how to avoid them
points: Vendor lock-in. Backups in a proprietary format, licences tied to the provider's account, and scripts only their engineers understand. Ask for open export formats and documentation of every custom script before notice.
Incomplete backups. Backup jobs that silently skipped Teams, SharePoint, laptops or a cloud application, or retention that was shorter than you assumed. Only a restore test reveals this.

Forgotten accounts. Old admin logins, service accounts, vendor portals and a domain registrar account tied to the provider's email address. Any of these can stay active for years after the contract ends.
Rushed migrations. A cutover squeezed into the last week of the notice period, often just before month-end close or a long Eid or National Day weekend, when nobody is around to fix what breaks.

sections.heading: Rushed exit versus planned exit
paragraphs: The checklist

Old provider cut off before the new team has admin access

No written confirmation that copies were deleted
Business-owned admin accounts created before notice
Overlap period with both providers working together

sections.heading: IT provider exit checklist: before, during and after the transition
paragraphs: Use this checklist as the working document for your exit. Give each item an owner and a date, tick it off only when there is evidence, and keep the completed list with your handover records. The timeline below shows how the three phases usually line up against your notice period.

paragraphs: Proof that the exit is finished, kept on file.

Reconcile final invoices and cancel leftover subscriptions

Hold a 30-day review and close every open item
Archive the exit file: handover list, test results, deletion confirmation

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions
paragraphs: Your business owns its data. The provider only processes it on your behalf. The practical issue is control: if accounts, subscriptions or backups were set up in the provider's name, you need them transferred to your company before you can use that ownership. Checking this early is the single most useful step in any exit.

A professional provider should not, and most contracts include handover obligations. Under the UAE PDPL, a processor is expected to erase or return personal data when processing ends. If a provider delays, put your requests in writing with dates, refer to the contract clauses, and involve your legal adviser if it continues. Having your own Global Administrator account in place before notice removes most of this risk.

No. Plan an overlap so both providers work during the notice period. The incoming team needs time to confirm access, run backups and verify data, and the outgoing team needs to be available to answer questions. Remove the old provider's access only after the new environment has been checked.

Usually not. If the tenant is registered to your company, your email, files and Teams data stay where they are. You change the administrators, remove the old provider's partner relationship and delegated access, and move your licence billing to the new partner. A tenant migration is only needed when the old provider set the tenant up under its own name.

It should list the data sets deleted, every system and backup location covered, the method used, the completion date and who performed the work. It should also name anything retained, why it was kept and when it will be deleted, and it should be signed by an authorised person at the provider.

For personal data under the federal PDPL, a processor is expected to erase the data or return it when processing ends. Companies in DIFC or ADGM follow their own free zone data protection rules, and health data falls under Federal Law No. 2 of 2019, which generally requires storage in the UAE and retention for at least 25 years. Write the deletion requirement into your exit request either way, and take legal advice for regulated data.

Service accounts and API keys behind integrations, the domain registrar login, backup encryption keys, remote support agents left on laptops, and old admin accounts with generic names. These rarely appear on a handover list unless you ask for them by name, which is why they sit in the checklist above.

title: SLA in IT Support Explained: What UAE Businesses Should Demand Before Signing a Contract
metaTitle: SLA in IT Support: What You Should Know | Rounak Computers LLC
excerpt: Learn what UAE businesses should demand in an IT support SLA, from response time and uptime to security, backups, escalation, and service accountability.
intro: In many UAE businesses, IT runs quietly in the background until something breaks. Then everything stops. Emails freeze, systems slow down, customers notice. That is usually the moment people realize they never really checked what their IT provider promised to deliver.
This is where a Service Level Agreement, or SLA, comes in. It is not just a contract. It is a practical document that defines how your IT partner behaves when things go wrong.
If you are working with an IT support company in Dubai, your SLA is the difference between fast recovery and long hours of frustration.

sections.heading: Why SLAs Matter More Than Most Businesses Think
paragraphs: Most companies sign IT agreements quickly. The focus is often on pricing or services listed. The actual performance details are skipped.

That becomes risky, especially if your business depends on cloud solutions in Dubai. Cloud systems need constant uptime and fast support. Without clear expectations written down, delays become normal instead of exceptions.
An SLA removes that ambiguity. It sets the ground rules before problems happen.

sections.heading: What You Should Clearly Demand in an SLA
paragraphs: A proper SLA is built on specific, measurable terms. Not general promises.
Start with these:
Response timeHow quickly does someone acknowledge your issue? Minutes or hours matter here.
Resolution timeFixing the issue is what actually counts. A fast reply means nothing if the problem stays unresolved.
Uptime commitmentIf your systems are built on AWS cloud service, you need a clear uptime percentage. Anything below expectations directly affects your operations.
Escalation structureWhat happens if the issue is not resolved? Who steps in next? If this is not defined, issues can sit unresolved longer than they should.

sections.heading: Security and Backup Are Not Optional
paragraphs: Cyber risks are increasing, and many businesses underestimate how exposed they are. An SLA should never treat security as an add-on.
If your setup includes tools like sophos firewall, your SLA must define how threats are monitored and handled. Who responds to a breach? How fast?
Data protection is another area where clarity matters. If you rely on data backup services Dubai the agreement should clearly state how often backups happen and how quickly data can be restored.
Backing up data is easy. Restoring it under pressure is where things fail if the SLA is weak.

sections.heading: Managed Services Need Stronger SLAs
paragraphs: When businesses move to IT managed services Dubai, they hand over more control. That makes the SLA even more important.
A good agreement should spell out:
For companies using tools like Microsoft 365 in Dubai, even short disruptions can impact communication and productivity. Your SLA should reflect how critical these systems are.
points: What exactly is covered
What is not included

sections.heading: Cloud Environments Change the Game

Many IT maintenance companies in Dubai offer similar services on paper. The SLA is what actually separates a reliable partner from a risky one.

title: UAE E-Invoicing: The IT Readiness Checklist Before Your ASP Deadline
metaTitle: UAE e-invoicing requirements and IT readiness | Rounak Computers | Rounak Computers LLC
excerpt: UAE e-invoicing requirements for IT teams: firms over AED 50m need an ASP by 30 October 2026. Get ERP data and integrations ready with Rounak Computers.

sections.heading: Structured data, not a PDF: what actually changes inside your systems
paragraphs: The UAE Electronic Invoicing System replaces document exchange with data exchange. For an IT team, that lands as three concrete changes: invoices leave your ERP as structured XML in the Peppol PINT AE profile, they travel through an Accredited Service Provider (ASP) instead of by email, and the tax data reaches the Federal Tax Authority along the same path. A PDF attached to an email stops being an invoice under the system, however neat the template looks.

The framework sits in Ministerial Decision No. 243 of 2025 and Ministerial Decision No. 244 of 2025, with penalties set by Cabinet Decision No. 106 of 2025. The Ministry of Finance published version 1.1 of the Electronic Invoicing Guidelines on 1 June 2026, which is the document your project should be working from. The model itself is a Peppol based decentralised continuous transaction control and exchange arrangement, usually described as the five corner model.
points: Invoices must be issued as structured XML using the PINT AE profile, not as PDF or scanned images.
Exchange runs through an ASP that you appoint, on both the sending and the receiving side.
Tax data is reported to the FTA as part of that same exchange, not as a separate filing.
Scope covers B2B and B2G transactions whether or not you are VAT registered, free zone entities included, while B2C sits outside the mandate for now.

sections.heading: Three dates decide your project plan
points: 1 July 2026 Pilot and voluntary adoption open Any business meeting the technical requirements can join early, and voluntary adopters are not exposed to the e-invoicing penalties before their own mandate date.

1 January 2027 Mandatory go-live for the first group The extension to the appointment deadline did not move this date, so the extra three months are preparation time, not slack in the plan.

sections.heading: What slipping costs
paragraphs: Penalties under Cabinet Decision No. 106 of 2025 apply once you are formally mandated, not during voluntary use. Failing to implement the system or appoint a provider on time carries AED 5,000 for each month or part month of delay. Invoices or credit notes that are not transmitted on time attract AED 100 each, capped at AED 5,000 per calendar month. Failing to notify the authority of a system failure within the prescribed window runs at AED 1,000 per day, and the same daily amount applies if you do not tell your provider about changes to your registered data.
System check

sections.heading: Can your ERP or accounting system actually produce this?
paragraphs: Start with a gap analysis rather than a vendor demo. The question is not whether your system prints invoices, it is whether it can hold and emit every required field in the right structure, for every transaction type you run.
points: Can it generate XML in the PINT AE profile, or does it stop at PDF and CSV export?
Does it cover tax invoices, credit notes, self-billed documents and commercial invoices for out-of-scope supplies?
Can it hold buyer identifiers, endpoint IDs and the code lists the schema expects?
Does it support advance payment linking and retention billing as version 1.1 describes them?
Can it receive inbound invoices from your suppliers, not only send them?

sections.heading: Legacy and small business software
paragraphs: Older packages and custom-built billing tools often have no native XML generation. Bridging that usually means a version upgrade, a connector supplied by the provider, or middleware sitting between the ledger and the network.

sections.heading: Invoices born outside the ERP
paragraphs: Point of sale terminals, booking portals, e-commerce checkouts and the spreadsheet a branch office quietly uses all count as invoice sources. Every one of them needs a route into the compliant flow or a decision to retire it.

sections.heading: Multiple entities and free zones
paragraphs: Each legal entity carries its own tax registration and its own connection. Group structures spread across emirates or free zones need their tax treatment and configuration settled per entity, not once for the group.

Where the honest answer is that the finance platform is at end of life, the e-invoicing deadline is a reasonable trigger to deal with that properly. Businesses replatforming at the same time often pair the compliance work with moving the ERP onto managed cloud infrastructure, so the new integration is built once against the environment they intend to keep.
Data first

sections.heading: Invoice data comes before integration
paragraphs: Most delays trace back to master data, not to XML. The connection can be perfect and still fail validation because a customer record is missing an identifier or an address is stored as free text.

The FTA technical guidance published in February 2026 sets out 51 mandatory fields for an electronic tax invoice, with an adapted set for commercial electronic invoices. Those fields are not free text. Country codes follow ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, units of measure follow UNECE Recommendation 20, dates follow the YYYY-MM-DD pattern, and the buyer is addressed by a participant identifier built from the scheme code 0235 and the 10 digit tax identification number.

Not every buyer will be onboarded on day one. The guidelines define predefined endpoints for those cases, including 0235:9900000098 where the buyer has no participant identifier, 0235:9900000097 for deemed supply, and 0235:9900000099 for exports where the buyer holds no Peppol ID.

Practically, this means a master data clean-up before any technical work: validate tax registration numbers, standardise legal names and address fields, remove duplicate customer and supplier records, align item and service descriptions, and agree the tax treatment for exports, free zone supplies, intercompany billing and self-billing arrangements. That work is slow, it involves the sales and procurement teams, and it cannot be compressed into the final fortnight.

sections.heading: Selecting and onboarding your Accredited Service Provider
Shortlist from the official list
paragraphs: Accredited providers are published by the Ministry of Finance and the Federal Tax Authority. Anyone not on that list cannot carry your invoices.

sections.heading: Test the technical fit
paragraphs: Ask for the integration method that suits your ERP, a sandbox, and evidence of work with systems like yours rather than a generic capability statement.

sections.heading: Appoint and onboard
paragraphs: The appointment is registered through EmaraTax, after which onboarding, identifier registration and configuration begin with the provider.

sections.heading: Integrate and validate
paragraphs: Map fields, generate sample documents, run validation against the schema and confirm the reporting acknowledgements come back as expected.

Accreditation is not a light process on the provider side either: applicants must hold active Peppol certification, meet information security and business continuity standards including ISO 27001 and ISO 22301, satisfy company and tax registration conditions, and show that their solution has been in operation for at least two years. The Ministry has indicated the review itself can take up to 90 working days, which is one reason the accredited list grew gradually rather than all at once.
Due diligence

sections.heading: Questions worth asking before you sign
paragraphs: Plumbing
points: Integration method, which connector, API or middleware applies to our exact ERP version, and who builds it.

Rejection handling, what does a validation failure look like in our system, and who is alerted.
Inbound flow, how do supplier invoices arrive in our accounts payable process, and in what format.
Volumes and peaks, what throughput is contracted, and what happens at month end.
Support model, working hours, escalation path and named response times after go-live.
Data handling, where records are hosted, how long they are kept, and how we retrieve them.
Exit, how we extract historic invoice data if we change provider later.

sections.heading: The transmission path, and the IT work it hides
paragraphs: Once the invoice leaves your ledger it is somebody else's traffic, which is exactly why the handover points deserve attention during build rather than during go-live week.
points: Outbound access from the finance environment to the provider endpoints, allowed through the firewall and documented

sections.heading: Write the outage runbook before you need it
paragraphs: Systems fail, and the rules anticipate it. A failure has to be notified to the authority within the prescribed window, two business days, and late notification carries a daily penalty. Invoices held during the outage are exchanged and reported once service resumes. The runbook should name who declares an incident, who notifies, what interim record is kept, and how the backlog is released in order once the link is restored. Agree it in writing with your provider so nobody assumes the other side is doing the notifying.
Storage and security

sections.heading: Where the invoice records live, and for how long
paragraphs: Version 1.1 of the guidelines confirmed that hosting offshore or in the cloud is acceptable provided the records stay complete and can be retrieved and reproduced for the FTA on request. Retention runs to five years after the relevant tax period for taxable persons, and seven years from the end of the calendar year for real estate records. Responsibility for archiving stays with the taxpayer even when a provider holds the data.

That makes the hosting decision a design choice rather than a formality, and it sits alongside the wider UAE data localisation and privacy rules your organisation already works under. Around the archive itself, the usual controls apply and are worth checking off deliberately: encryption in transit, restricted access by role, logged retrieval, backups that are tested, and the email and endpoint security that keeps invoice fraud away from the same finance mailboxes.

sections.heading: Who owns what inside the business
paragraphs: Treating this as an IT project is the most expensive mistake available, and it is a common one. The technical build is perhaps a third of the work. The rest is tax interpretation, master data and daily operating habits, which is why a named project owner and an agreed split of responsibilities matter more than the tooling.

sections.heading: Tax and finance
paragraphs: Scope, phase and exemptions, transaction treatment, invoice controls and reconciliation after go-live.

sections.heading: IT and ERP
paragraphs: Field mapping, integration and connectivity, environments, monitoring, certificates and access control.

sections.heading: Accounts receivable and payable
paragraphs: Day to day issuing and receiving, rejection queues, corrections and resubmission, supplier chasing.

sections.heading: Procurement, legal and the project lead
paragraphs: Customer and supplier readiness, provider contracts and data terms, deadline tracking and issue escalation.

Smaller finance teams in Dubai rarely have spare hands for a programme like this on top of daily support, which is where an IT annual maintenance contract tends to absorb the monitoring and endpoint side while the internal team concentrates on invoice logic.

sections.heading: Technical mistakes that surface late
points: Assuming the current invoice template is enough. A human readable layout is not a machine readable document, and existing templates rarely carry every mandatory field.
Leaving master data until after integration. Missing identifiers and inconsistent legal names fail validation no matter how good the connection is.
Testing only outbound flows. Receiving compliant invoices from suppliers changes the accounts payable process just as much as issuing changes billing.
Forgetting invoice sources outside the ERP. Point of sale, portals and manual spreadsheets are in scope even when they were never part of the finance stack.
Treating the appointment date as the finish line. Appointing a provider in October is not the same as being integrated and tested by January.
No owner for failed transmissions. Rejections that nobody is alerted to become penalties that arrive quietly, month after month.

paragraphs: Businesses with annual revenue of AED 50 million or more must appoint one by 30 October 2026, a date extended from the original 31 July 2026. Businesses below that threshold and in-scope government entities have until 31 March 2027. The appointment is registered through EmaraTax, and only providers on the Ministry of Finance and Federal Tax Authority accredited lists can be used.

In most cases yes, provided it can produce the mandatory fields in a structured form and connect to your provider, directly or through middleware. The test is not the brand of the system but whether it can hold every required data element, cover all your document types and transaction scenarios, and both send and receive. Older or heavily customised systems often need an upgrade, a connector or an integration layer.

Not on their own. Once your phase becomes mandatory, a valid invoice is a structured XML document in the PINT AE profile exchanged through an accredited provider. A PDF can still be produced for human readers alongside it, but it carries no compliance value by itself, and neither do scans, images or email attachments.

Version 1.1 of the guidelines allows offshore and cloud hosting as long as records remain complete and can be retrieved and reproduced for the Federal Tax Authority. Retention is five years after the relevant tax period for taxable persons, extending to seven years from the end of the calendar year for real estate records. Archiving responsibility stays with the taxpayer even when a provider stores the data on your behalf.

A system failure has to be reported to the authority within the prescribed window of two business days, and late notification carries a penalty of AED 1,000 per day. Invoices held during the outage are transmitted and reported once service resumes. Agree in advance who declares the incident, who notifies, and how the backlog is released, so both you and your provider are not each waiting for the other.

The system applies broadly to B2B and B2G transactions regardless of VAT registration status, and free zone entities are included where their transactions fall within scope. Purely B2C sales sit outside the mandate for now. A handful of exclusions exist, including certain sovereign government activities, some international air transport services and VAT exempt or zero rated financial services.

Cabinet Decision No. 106 of 2025 sets AED 5,000 for each month or part month of delay in implementing the system or appointing a provider, AED 100 for each invoice or credit note not transmitted on time capped at AED 5,000 per calendar month, and AED 1,000 per day for failing to notify a system failure or a change in registered data on time. Penalties apply from your mandatory date, not during voluntary use.

paragraphs: If the checklist turned up more red items than green, the technical half of the work is the part that can be planned and staffed. Our engineers in Bur Dubai have handled ERP connectivity, environment setup and monitoring for UAE businesses since 2004.

title: Still Running Windows 10? ESU Costs and Your Options in 2026
metaTitle: Windows 10 ESU cost 2026 and upgrade options | Rounak Computers | Rounak Computers LLC
excerpt: Windows 10 ESU cost 2026: year 2 is $122 per business PC after 13 October. Weigh renewal against a Windows 11 upgrade or new hardware with Rounak Computers.

sections.heading: Extended Security Updates are a security bridge, not a support renewal
paragraphs: Windows 10 reached end of support on 14 October 2025. The machines did not stop working that day and they still have not. What stopped was the free flow of security patches. Microsoft's Extended Security Updates programme, ESU, is the paid route that puts those patches back on an eligible Windows 10 PC while you plan the move to Windows 11.

The distinction matters more than the price tag. ESU delivers the critical and important security updates defined by the Microsoft Security Response Center for devices running Windows 10, version 22H2. It does not reopen feature development, it does not bring back non-security fixes, and it does not restore general technical support. Microsoft confirms that ESU provides security updates but does not add new features or extend general technical support.
For a business in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE, that means ESU is a line item with an expiry date attached, not a way to keep an ageing fleet indefinitely.
Eligibility

sections.heading: There are two ESU programmes, and your device only fits one
paragraphs: This is the single most common point of confusion, and it is where most people get their budget wrong. Microsoft runs a consumer programme for personal devices and a separate commercial programme sold through volume licensing. They differ in price, in length, and in who can use them. A domain-joined office PC cannot buy its way into the cheap consumer route, no matter who is sitting in front of it.

Managed through MDM. Anything enrolled in a mobile device management solution falls outside the consumer programme.

Already licensed. A device that already holds an ESU licence cannot enrol again.
Account type. Enrolment requires an administrator Microsoft account. Local-account users are prompted to sign in, and child accounts do not qualify.

sections.heading: Windows 10 ESU cost in 2026: the three published rates
paragraphs: Microsoft publishes ESU pricing in US dollars. Buyers in the UAE pay the local currency equivalent plus applicable VAT, and business licences are usually invoiced in dirhams by a local partner or cloud solution provider rather than bought directly from Microsoft.

sections.heading: The commercial price ladder, and why late enrolment costs more
paragraphs: Commercial ESU is cumulative. An organisation that skips Year 1 and enrols in Year 2 pays for both years, so the entry price becomes $183 per device rather than $122.

There is one route that carries no ESU charge at all. Windows 10 virtual machines running in Windows 365, Azure Virtual Desktop, Azure Virtual Machines and several other Azure services are entitled to ESU at no additional cost, and Windows 10 endpoints connecting to a Windows 365 Cloud PC are covered for up to three years with an active subscription. For UAE businesses already weighing a desktop-as-a-service model, that entitlement can change the arithmetic completely, which is worth raising with whoever handles your Microsoft Azure services before you buy a single ESU licence.

paragraphs: That last point catches people out. Browser makers, accounting packages and line-of-business vendors set their own support policies, and several have already drawn a line at Windows 10. An ESU licence patches the operating system, it does not oblige anyone else to keep testing against it. Pairing ESU with layered endpoint protection is a sensible interim posture, and it is one of the reasons a Windows 10 holdout fleet usually needs tighter security solutions around it rather than looser ones.

paragraphs: Confirm the PC runs Windows 10, version 22H2, and install every pending Windows update.

The decision

sections.heading: Renew, upgrade, replace, or run unpatched
paragraphs: Every organisation still holding Windows 10 devices in 2026 is choosing between four paths, whether or not the choice has been made explicitly. Doing nothing is one of them.

Upgrading in place is the cheapest outcome when the hardware qualifies, because Windows 11 carries its own support lifecycle and no per-year fee. The trap is assuming eligibility. A device that runs Windows 10 comfortably can still fail the Windows 11 check on firmware alone.

Where the hardware genuinely cannot make the jump, replacement often beats a multi-year ESU commitment once you total the ladder. A device kept on ESU for the full three years absorbs $427 before you count the staff time spent maintaining it, which is frequently within touching distance of a new business desktop. If you are pricing that comparison, it is worth getting current UAE quotes on business hardware alongside the licensing numbers rather than after them.

For UAE businesses

sections.heading: What changes when you are covering thirty devices, not three
paragraphs: The practical answer for most SMEs is to stop treating this as a one-off purchase. Enrolment, key deployment, patch verification and the eventual migration are recurring operational tasks with hard dates attached, which is exactly the kind of work that sits naturally inside an IT annual maintenance contract rather than being handled ad hoc each October.
Decision guide
points: The consumer route is off the table. Once devices are domain joined or managed through Intune, the $30 option disappears and commercial licensing applies to every one of them.
Prices are quoted in dollars, invoiced in dirhams. Budget for the local currency equivalent plus applicable VAT, and confirm the exchange basis your partner uses before approving the purchase order.
Management tooling earns a discount. Devices managed through Microsoft Intune or Windows Autopatch attract a reduced ESU rate, which is worth confirming if you already own the licences.

Partial fleets are normal. Most UAE SMEs find a mix: some devices upgrade cleanly, a few need firmware changes, and a small group is genuinely stuck behind an application or a piece of connected equipment.
Healthcare, education and government carry extra weight. In regulated environments an unpatched endpoint is not only a technical risk, it is a documentation problem at the next audit.

sections.heading: Which option is right for you?
Your devices pass the Windows 11 check
paragraphs: Upgrade in place and skip ESU entirely. Test your critical applications on one machine first, then roll out in waves. Paying for ESU on eligible hardware is money spent twice.

sections.heading: The hardware fails, and the devices are near end of life anyway
paragraphs: Replace rather than renew. One year of ESU on a five-year-old desktop buys twelve months on a machine that will still need replacing, and Year 2 doubles the bill.

sections.heading: A specific application or machine ties you to Windows 10
paragraphs: This is the case ESU was designed for. Buy Year 1 for the affected devices only, isolate them on the network, and set a firm date to resolve the dependency.

sections.heading: You are considering doing nothing
paragraphs: Understand what you are accepting. The device keeps working, but every vulnerability disclosed from now on stays open on it permanently. For a shared office PC handling client data, that is not a saving.

title: Barracuda vs Mimecast for UAE Businesses: Choosing an Email Security Layer
